column4: This ayah draws the conclusion from 22:5's human and earth stages: God is the Truth, gives life to the dead, and has power over all things.
The next ayah states the conclusion that the Hour will come and those in graves will be raised, completing the staged-creation argument cited by the section.
The question “Have you considered what you emit?” introduces the seed whose Creator is identified in 56:59, so its own contribution is the visible first material stage.
God creates the human from a drop, yet the formed human becomes an open adversary; the compressed beginning-to-denial arc closely matches the section's closing rebuke.
God begins creation and repeats it in order to reward believers who do right, directly joining first formation, return, and recompense.
God begins creation, repeats it, and then people return to Him, a concise statement of the full trajectory beyond bodily decline.
God promises to repeat creation just as He began the first creation, making origination itself the measure of resurrection.
كَمَا بَدَأَكُمْ تَعُودُونَ states that people return as God began them, directly linking first state and final return.
At death the person asks, “My Lord, return me,” making the cutoff of life the point at which a wished-for reversal becomes impossible.
The requested return is for doing righteousness in the life left behind, but a barrier remains until resurrection; this sharply distinguishes finite opportunity from the later outcome.
God knows every pregnancy, what wombs diminish or increase, and every thing has its measure; this directly joins gestation to precise determination.
Knowledge of what is in wombs and where a soul will die places hidden human origin and hidden endpoint within one ayah.
God knows people when He brings them from earth and while they are embryos in their mothers' wombs, spanning material origin and concealed formation.
A pregnancy passes from a light burden to heaviness before the parents ask for a sound child, supplying a distinct internal progression within the womb stage.
The mother bears the child in weakness upon weakness and weans it in two years, adding measured infancy and maternal bodily change to the lifetime image.
Before death arrives, the dying person wishes for a brief delay in order to give and become righteous; the ayah connects life's cutoff to deeds that would affect the lasting outcome.
Against the grateful mature person of 46:15, this grown child scoffs at the promise of being brought out after death, showing denial as one possible outcome of reaching maturity.
The painful punishment announced after stage-followed-by-denial stands opposite the unceasing reward in 84:25, completing that passage's two outcomes.
A Day that makes children gray-haired catastrophically compresses the ordinary childhood-to-grayness trajectory and locates that reversal at Judgment.
Zechariah says old age has reached him and his wife is barren; the closed reproductive stage becomes the setting for God's power to create new life.
Extreme old age and a barren wife appear as bodily limits to be crossed by the promised child, illuminating senescence without making it ultimate.
An old woman with an elderly husband wonders at bearing a child, setting age's ordinary decline in fertility against divine creation.
Worldly life is temporary enjoyment while the Hereafter is the lasting home, directly setting the finite span against what endures after it.
The worldly life is play and diversion while the Hereafter is the true life, a boundary between passing stages and lasting existence.
God creates the male and female pair before 53:46 identifies the emitted drop, so this ayah contributes differentiation within completed human form.
Orphans are tested until marriageable age and property is released when sound judgment appears, making maturation a threshold of capacity and responsibility.
When children reach puberty, their rule of seeking permission changes to the adult rule, showing a bodily stage carrying a new social status.
Two complete years of nursing provide a measured early-life interval after birth, complementing the womb stages emphasized in the section.
Reaching full strength marks the point at which an orphan's property may be approached differently, giving maturity a concrete legal consequence.
The protection of an orphan's property lasts until full strength is reached, again treating maturity as a distinct threshold rather than an undivided lifespan.
The two orphans are to reach full strength before extracting their treasure, making bodily maturity the appointed point of independent action.
God announces the creation of a mortal from clay before 15:29 describes proportioning him, so this ayah supplies that formed body's material beginning.
The announced creation of a human from clay precedes the proportioning in 38:72 and thus contributes the initial material stage of the same sequence.
After a sound child is granted in 7:189, the recipients associate partners with God; its own contribution is denial following the successful completion of gestation.
In a resurrection dispute, the addressees are reminded that God created them from sticky clay, using their first material origin to test the claim that renewed creation is difficult.
God increased the people in physical stature, a direct bodily-height parallel to the section's dictionary gloss of qiwām as completeness and length.
Saul is increased in knowledge and body, pairing mature bodily amplitude with knowledge at the life-course summit before senile loss.
Nightly taking and daytime raising continue until a named term, after which return and accounting come; the daily cycle models a bounded life and final return.
Those judged acknowledge two deaths and two lives, retrospectively recognizing that earthly death was one transition rather than the last state.
Rain revives earth after its death, another direct recurrence of the secondary field scene that 22:5 uses as evidence.
Rain gives life to earth after its death as a sign for people who reason, repeating the visible revival stage without explicitly naming human resurrection in this ayah.
Provision descends from the sky and revives earth after death within a list of signs, preserving the same secondary natural parallel.
Rain revives the earth after death and spreads creatures through it; this is a broad sign-scene corresponding to the revived field in 22:5.
Water revives a dead land and gives drink to creatures; its relevance is the revived-land scene itself, while the ayah does not explicitly draw the resurrection inference.
Flood foam vanishes while what benefits people remains on earth, a physical parable for the section's contrast between what is cut off and what endures.
The garden promised to the mindful has lasting fruit and shade, giving concrete continuity to recompense beyond the changing body.
God begins creation and repeats it, a repeated direct formulation of the inference from first formation to later origination.
The question asks which supposed partner can begin creation and then repeat it, and answers that God does both.
Beginning creation and repeating it appear among the acts by which false partners are challenged, reinforcing the same creation-to-return inference.
إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ يُبْدِئُ وَيُعِيدُ compresses beginning and repetition into a single divine action pair.
The production of fire from a green tree supplies a concrete transformation immediately after the answer about reviving decayed bones.
The Creator of heavens and earth is declared able to create the like of humans, continuing the answer to the objection from bodily decay.
A single blast answers the preceding question about return from decayed bones; its own contribution is the effortless event that initiates restoration.
After that blast, the dead are suddenly on the open surface, supplying the actual restored state denied in 79:10–11.
The condemned are reminded that they were given a life long enough to take warning, making completed lifespan the evidence that precedes judgment.
